{{nihongo|'''Taimasan Shrine'''|大麻山神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Iwami Province]].

'''Ōasayama Shrine''' (おおあさやまじんじゃ, also read たいまさんじんじゃ) is a Shinto shrine located in Misumi-chō, {{ill|Hamada, Shimane|Q432055|qid=Q432055}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|Q132751|qid=Q132751}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}}, and its former shrine rank was {{ill|Gō-sha|Q134917316|qid=Q134917316}}.

There was a Buddhist temple, Sonshō-ji, serving as the shrine-temple ({{ill|Jingū-ji|fr|Jingū-ji|it|Jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺|pl|Jingū-ji|ru|Дзингудзи|zh|神宮寺|qid=Q1074971}}), and it was called the “Kōyasan of the West.” However, in the seventh year of {{ill|Tenpō|Q1369045|qid=Q1369045}} ({{ill|1836|ab|1836|af|1836|als|1836|am|1836 እ.ኤ.አ.|an|1836|ar|1836|ary|1836|arz|1836|ast|1836|avk|1836|az|1836|azb|۱۸۳۶ Furthermore, they were damaged in the Hamada earthquake of the fifth year of Meiji ({{ill|1872|Q7753|qid=Q7753|lt=1872}}). Influenced by the era of anti-Buddhist policies (haibutsu kishaku), Sonshō-ji was never rebuilt and became a ruined temple.

=== Enshrined deities ===
The enshrined deities are {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ame-no-Hiwashi-no-Mikoto}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Sarutahiko-no-Mikoto}}, and Ōasa-hiko-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Futodama|it|Futodama|ja|フトダマ|ru|Футодама|simple|Futodama|zh|布刀玉命|qid=Q11059539|lt=Ame-no-Futodama-no-Mikoto}}). In addition, {{ill|Zaō Gongen|cs|Zaó gongen|de|Zaō Gongen|ja|蔵王権現|zh|藏王權現|qid=Q10514059}}, {{ill|Kumano Gongen|ja|熊野権現|simple|Kumano Gongen|zh|熊野權現|qid=Q11568925}}, {{ill|Izusan Gongen|ja|伊豆山権現|qid=Q11380566|lt=Hashiyu Gongen}}, {{ill|Sannō Gongen|Q11470054|qid=Q11470054}}, and {{ill|Hakusan Gongen|Q11579578|qid=Q11579578}} are jointly enshrined, and the shrine came to be called the Five-Gongen Shrine.

=== History ===
Ōasayama was originally called Twin Mountains. In the fourth year of {{ill|Ninna|Q1346317|qid=Q1346317}} (888), following a divine oracle, it was renamed Ōasayama, and this was reported to the imperial court. In the first year of {{ill|Kanpyō (era)|Q1346292|qid=Q1346292}} ({{ill|889|Q23833|qid=Q23833|lt=889}}), the great deity enshrined at Mount Ōasa in {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|Q907457|qid=Q907457}} ({{ill|Tokushima Prefecture|Q160734|qid=Q160734}}), {{ill|Itano District, Tokushima|Q1156025|qid=Q1156025}}, was invited, and with the imperial permission of {{ill|Emperor Uda|Q349267|qid=Q349267}}, a shrine building was constructed.

=== Legend ===
Led by Ōasa-hiko-no-Mikoto, the {{ill|Inbe clan|Q8189229|qid=Q8189229|lt=Imbe tribe}} migrated from Awa Province. Ōasa-hiko-no-Mikoto crossed the sea on horseback and traveled through the mountains by boat. Upon entering Ōasayama, Ōasa-hiko-no-Mikoto drove away the Ono clan, who lived on the nearby Ono Plain, by throwing rocks at them. The Ono clan fled as far as {{ill|Mount Kōyama|Q11669293|qid=Q11669293|lt=Takayama}} in Susa and retaliated by throwing rocks, but they only reached the foothills of Ōasayama. Eventually, a mediator appeared, the Ono clan returned to Ono, and the dispute was settled with the Imbe clan taking Ōasayama as their territory.<ref>“The passage titled ‘The Battle of Ōasayama and Takayama,’ included in the following ‘Myths and Legends of the Misumi Region’ (edited by Misumi Jihōsha), was written by the late Terai Jitsurō, who conducted on-site investigations while systematizing historical facts. As it skillfully weaves myth into history, it is reprinted here while praying for the repose of the deceased,” as stated in the Misumi Town History.</ref>

In the “History of Shimane Prefecture,” it is written: “In ancient times, a battle began between Ino Village and Ōasa Village, and stones bearing the marks of where heavenly horses galloped about still remain today on the mountainside of Ōasayama.”
